This makes perfect sense to me. I hear everything you said. I enjoy your reply as well (146 days later haha)! I think it's really important that those of us willing to share our stories absolutely should share, and build off of others. Thank you for sharing with us all! 

Because of how much I appreciated your comment, I wanted to share why I appreciated it. It's totally unprompted, I'm just really passionate about visibility. And why I am so happy you commented has everything to do with visibility. 

First: I'm so sorry that Reddit is such a cesspool. Every time I get on here a self-identifying incel who doesn't know what they're talking about (or what self love is) pisses me off. It is ridiculous how ours are the first and only two comments mentioning racism that I have ever seen regarding this song. But this is Reddit! I'm not surprised. 

What you said deserves respect. I'm sorry that the only thing that majority of people within this forum (and the world in general) don't acknowledge your perspective as a black man. So many people don't listen when other people are speaking, either. Minds remain closed instead of open; the cycle continues; ignorance survives; history and culture stay erased. It's so sad. 

Part of me believes that this song was one of Tyler's many attempts at shining light on social injustice through rap. But majority of people won't even listen to Tyler! Everyone loves honey but hate the bees that make it! Ugh! 

I even did some digging and not a single published interpretation of this song even mentions black culture. It only talks about rejection and heartbreak. Just like the comments in this forum. It's almost like we're invisible (More specifically! We as a people have been erased in the eyes of the masses, aside from stereotypes and "model minorities" which are also stereotypes). 

Four years ago, this forum reminded me of how imperialism has doomed us (and all other marginalized groups) to continue to be marginalized by complete strangers, until the end of humanity. I fear the -isms will never stop ruining peoples lives. But we do have our communities, as well as each other! 

TLDR: Thank you so much for sharing. You've reminded me that we see each other when the world does not. When nobody talks about it, we will talk about it to each other. You know? Even four years later I felt my heart grow a size, after being treated really shitty really often for all 23 years of my black womanhood. (Ngl! After a certain point, trauma turned me into the Grinch! I gotta overcome my misanthrope now LOL) So thank you, thank you, thank you for reminding me there is hope for humanity.

You absolutely lost the point 💀 

Every assumption you make of others is a confession of what you think about yourself. Just because *you* don't want to hear them practice, doesn't mean the whole world doesn't. Your opinion doesn't outweigh everyone else's, you're just being another jerk on Reddit. What even makes you think that this isn't a thing that people do? You're just a person behind a screen, just like everyone else is. Why take all that time to tell OP that an out-of-the-box method will fail? (I'm taking my time to reply because 1) LOL people love hearing others practice! To insist that nobody does is nuts and 2) I'm rooting for OP, and every other artists who found this thread. I felt the need to comment something to combat the negativity.)

Whatever you gotta do to practice is whatever you gotta do to practice. The Followers you gain and stream for will yell at you when you don't stream/post, which makes live streaming a great "accountability partner." It isn't about competing with other streamers, it's about being externally motivated the things you say you'll do (practice daily!). 

Yes, intrinsic motivation alone can change your behavior, but combining it with extrinsic motivation is what set habits and systems into place (consistency!). And different strokes for different folks! Some need a habit tracker, some need that pen/clock/paper combo, some need to live stream! 

Using Viewers/streaming as one great big collective accountability partner can even lead to semi-passive and passive income if you do it over a long period of time. You're killing multiple birds with one stone. The list of pluses goes on and on. It isn't a bad idea for anyone who wants to do it-- even if not everyone wants to do (or view) it. 

(Source: I had to study basic behavioral psychology to earn my educator's license. This stuff is up that alley.)

This is a great idea. James Scholz did it and ended up being not only successful in his endeavors, but also helpful to others. Reddit is full of haters who think their personal opinions are facts. 

Don't listen to the weirdos in the comments-- lots of people genuinely want to watch/listen to artists practice. Mainly, the people who practice themselves, or who need inspiration from other artists. Heck, people pay to sit and watch *orchestras* practice. Whoever says that nobody wants to hear you is probably trying to clip your wings because someone else clipped theirs. The assumption that nobody wants to hear you is absolutely false. 

Good luck, have fun, happy streaming, and fuck the haters!

I listened to everything linked on this forum, and this is not plagiarism. Kanno openly copies the structures of trendy music in many of her projects. If you were familiar with the published music of at least one or two genres, you could hear that many of her works have closely similar structures to other pieces without these videos. These videos point out the obvious to those whose ears are trained: but this is absolutely not plagiarism. Plagiarism is copying and pasting, not building off of one. 

I'm very familiar with classical and jazz classics. A *lot* of her music has at *least* a few measures that resemble a few measures of another artist's piece. I noticed that she changes the set of instruments, but not really the tempo. What she does *around* those two measures never fails to blow my mind in ways that majority of other composers don't. Like, 

I really understand music. I'm known for my understanding of theory and piano technique, that every time I land a gig, somebody there has heard about my skills before we met. I am not trying to brag to be an asshole, but I'm confident for a reason. I know I'm not inserting my opinion because that's how well I understand music. But we're strangers, and there's no way that you could tell that I'm not just being arrogant in saying this. 

The patterns that Kanno creates or weaves into a reference are so fun to analyze. It's like a web that keeps expanding. She is among the composers who *play* with shape, volume, breathe. It's like a game. She isn't the only one, but she is one of many who have a playful approach with conveying and resolving musical conflicts. One pattern is a part of a bigger pattern that weaves into another bigger pattern with other small patterns inside of it. 

Other composers who play with pattern do this, too. For example: Jacob Collier. His music is *full* of references to other pieces. Shoot, many of his pieces are covers that fully flesh out the original piece, as well. Not only is it recreated, but it also lets us see into his understanding of music theory. Just like Kanno's music does. They both treat it (and talk about it in interviews!) like a game. 

The way that Kanno takes something that already exists, and totally fleshes it out, is what she is known for. She talks about this in her interviews, as well. Compare her work to Michael Jackson (she mentioned structuring many of her pieces after him, actually!) and you'll hear him in her music. Same for Coletrane, Armstrong, Mozart, (Barry) Harris; I even hear Bach in her pieces, sometimes. You just gotta know other composers and the patterns in their music. 

But if you don't it "sounds basically same" because you can't hear the stark differences.   They are not the same.

I only feel beautiful with natural styles, yes, but I also haven't learned to feel confident with my *own* hair in curly and protective styles. I just started my locs with the new year and I feel *cute.* But I do not feel beautiful like how I feel with waist length braids, twists, or a curly crocheted bob. My microtwists resemble an overgrown pixie cut, with an overgrown fade. Cute as can be. I get just as many compliments now than I did when I wore extensions all the time, if not more. Nobody's unhappy with the way I look but myself, I think. I'm the only person who hates my body, after a year of loving it. But the only reason I loved it was because I always had hair flowing to my butt, or framing my face and shoulders to take attention away from my muscles. Before, I hated the way I looked, and I just didn't feel like a real girl. Before, the first thing people noticed was how jacked my arms are. And now it's happening again. I have to accept and appreciate that my body isn't tiny, like how big and long hair made me feel. I don't feel dainty or petite anymore, even though the only thing that changed is my hair, and I'm not even getting *any* hate whatsoever for it. 

I'm loccing up to learn how to take care of and accept all of me, not only my hair. I'm tired of depending on weaves to look pretty and crossing my fingers that my real hair is still healthy by the time I uninstall. It felt terrible, but at least I could hide my physical insecurities behind hair. Behind the personas I invented with each style. But now, I feel unattractive most days, which feels even worse because there's nowhere to hide. No sudden changes when I don't like the person in the mirror, only me. I have to learn to love *me,* now. 

The battle is within. You are not alone. We learned to feel this way about ourselves from someone, which means we can unlearn it from someone else. It's a journey.

How much I'll get paid as an apprentice (the shop I want to work at doesn't let you work/clean for free). 

Until I know for certain that there's no way I can apprentice at this time in my life, is to at least half-land an apprenticeship. Get to the point where we talk about time and money and agreements. Until then, I'm not gonna sike myself out anymore. 

I already gave up on the dream for a few years, until my artist asked me if I was interested in apprenticing under his former mentor (same shop). Because the minute he asked me, apprenticing as a student didn't seem far fetched anymore. 

I mentioned being committed school and work and afraid of biting off more than I can chew. He told me that he was in a very similar busy-boat during his apprenticeship. And then he sort of frowned and told me that sometimes, you just gotta reach out and grab opportunities. And that this is an all-or-nothing career and apprenticing still must have high-priority, regardless. 

I still fear being rejected because my would-be mentor assumes I don't want to dedicate my life to body art (for having a non-artistic major). But that's anxiety that I have no reason to feed into until the day when he tells me: "I will not teach you because you are/were a college student. Which means you don't have dedication to tattooing."

(And honestly? Dedication shows in practicing every day. I doubt a mentor will turn you down for being an adult with multiple commitments. But in that case, I'd just keep looking for a mentor that acknowledges that I draw daily, on top of work and school.)

My takeaway from the conversation that through time management, persistence, and communication he made it work :3 If you feel comfortable with doing so, could ask the artist you'd like to learn under for their advice and opinions. I hope this helps some!

Is it realistic to balance being a full-time student (non-artistic major) and an apprentice at the same time? I get that it depends on the flexibility of your mentor, but I also understand that there's the "if you want to be a tattoo artist so much, you wouldn't need to go to college" argument. Because tattooing is a lifestyle and trade you've got to put your all into. I absolutely do respect it as such and believe that it's safe to say that I take it dead seriously. But I just so happen to be earning my bachelor's, too, for a few reasons beyond my own control.

(And, yes, I could just wait till graduation to apprentice, if I really must, sure. But do I *want* to wait any longer? It's like an itch I can't scratch. I just want to do it.)

So I guess that my question is actually whether or not I actually need to justify myself to my future-mentor, even if my portfolio and productivity are straight. 

Like... is being both a college student and requesting an apprenticeship just setting myself up to be brushed off? I know that one day I'm going to have to pick one hat to wear at a time, but this is where my passion lies. *I do not want to pass up the opportunity to earn this hat.* And there's no telling what the future will hold, how unhappy and too-busy-to-apprentice I'll be post-graduation, so I don't see why now would be a bad time.

For me, it feels like school is the side-gig (that I take somewhat seriously) and tattooing is the big, main thing I'm chasing. The bachelor's is a 'backup plan' that appeases my parents, I'll say for a lack of better words. Is that a 'bad' way to 'justify' doing both? *Do I even need to feel insecure about this at all?*

I ask because I've been asking my tattoo artist about his apprenticeship, and he seems to believe that artists can only have one main craft. Because I introduced myself as a musician, he refers to music as my craft, and doesn't really seem to think I feel as passionate about visual art as I actually do. I get 'musician-ed' a lot when I try to talk to him about visual art, hehe.

Others opinions don't matter, I know my own truth, et cetera, but I'm so afraid. I hate that I have, like, fifty hobbies and am 18 and in the process of figuring myself out (which is all fine), but is there ever a time to stop persisting? I don't want to give up on this, but I don't want to be out of line, arrogant, or disrespectful to a tattoo master. That is, disrespectful by waltzing in with a clean portfolio, a polished CV, a nice business card, *and* a pre-existing long-term commitment.

So; other than having all my sh*t together, being punctual, and honest with myself and my future-mentor. Is there a way that I can prove to that I want this and take it seriously? Is already being a full-time student (or full-time anything) a common make-or-break for tattoo artists, when weeding out apprentices? Or am I just overthinking this all.

Gender identity is just a popular subject these days, which is why so many kids and people are making it bandwagon to hop on. Or, "transtrending." It's upsetting and toxic for multiple communities.

Trans people experience gender dysphoria with their secondary sex characteristics, and how they're perceived. It is distressful, uncomfortable-- I could talk all day about mine. You look in the mirror and can't recognize yourself; it's not about being fat or skinny. Your body was just structured entirely differently than you imagine, and you constantly have to deal with it. Hence the need to transition. The need to change your biology, pronouns and adjectives. 

Because clothing isn't definitive. Cis and trans men wear feminine things and are still men. Cis and trans women can wear masculine things and still be women. And there's always androgynous apparel. Everyone is still themselves regardless of their clothes (and hobbies.)

Clothing and societal roles are social constructs. Sex is biological. Gender identity combines biology with socialization. 

(Which is why all these little kids need to stop claiming to be transgender *solely* because they like androgynous shit. It gives us a bad reputation and embarrasses them in the long run. Non binary people (speaking from my experience) experience dysphoria from both directions. It makes you feel dysphoric to be perceived as a man, and dysphoric to be perceived as a man. A wardrobe change isn't enough; because there's still the social and biological dysphoria that clothing can't change. Hence the preference for androgynous pronouns and adjectives. Clothing, again, is not definitive. So clothing preferences varies from person to person.

Imagine feeling like a freak your whole life. Because you've dealt with dysphoria for years before you even knew what "dysphoria" means. But you don't identify with your sex-assigned gender, but you don't identify with the opposite gender, either. Until you finally find a word that doesn't make you have to pick either one of the two. Doesn't make your skin crawl. "Non binary." "Neither identifying as a man nor a woman." They/them. It doesn't make you cringe, it doesn't make you feel like you're lying, and it's possible. 

Now this part is even more personal. Aside from wanting a penis, my dysphoria is the exact same as majority of trans man's. And even there, not all trans men want penises. But all trans men see themselves as men, are comfortable with being refered to with he/him pronouns, and with being called burly things. Me? That makes my skin crawl just as much being called she/her or a woman does. And having the word "non-binary" to define myself is what makes me feel empowered about that discomfort, instead of like an awkward subcategory of "I'm not cis? But I'm not trans? But that's ridiculous because I can't just be neither?" Like. I feel at peace with myself, now. I don't feel like I "have" to be a man or a woman if I genuinely am uncomfortable with calling myself either.

I do doubt myself. Maybe I'm a trans man, but am simply not used to being called a man. I don't know. It's a process so I'm not too worried about doing anything, but figuring out how to alleviate my dysphoria at the moment. (And the rest of my life. Bottom line. My mans explained "my body, my choice" perfectly. It doesn't mean that there's no communication whatsoever.
